en: The Tenth Prince’s Deeds—Third Chapter:
"Here I am; once, while wandering, I went to the Videha country.
Without even entering Mithilā, I stayed outside in a certain monastery."
Having arrived to rest, I was offered water for my feet by a certain elderly female ascetic and stayed for a moment on the terrace;
at the mere sight of me, however, she began to shed some kind of continuous stream [of tears].
Tears flowed forth.
When asked, "Mother, tell me, what is the cause of this?", she spoke piteously: "O long-lived one, has it not been heard that the husband..."
In this city of Mithilā, there was a man named Prahāravarmā;
he indeed had Rājahamsa, the king of Magadha, as his closest friend.
And those two, Vasumatī and Priyaṃvadā, formed an incomparable friendship, like that of Bala and Śambalā;
then, she was greeted with joy at her first pregnancy.
Desiring to see her dear friend, Priyamvadā went with her husband to Puṣpapura to visit Vasumatī;
and at that very time, there was a great conflict between Mālava and the King of Magadha.
The son was born;
yet, regarding that event, the King of Magadha could not perceive even the slightest sign of its course.
The King of Mithilā, however, having been restored to life through the efforts of the King of Mālava,
returned toward his own territory, accompanied by the sons of his elder brother Saṃhāravarman, headed by Vikaṭavarman.
Having heard that his kingdom was occupied by his sister's son, the lord of Suhma,
he entered a forest path desiring to seize a portion of the army;
however, his entire property was plundered by hunters.
And together with her youngest son, who was by my side, I fled alone out of fear of the shower of arrows from the forest-dwellers and entered the forest;
and there, while I had fallen, having been mangled by the claws of a tiger—
Slipping from his hand, the boy hid himself in the lap of a certain brown cow-calf;
and the arrow took the life of the tiger that was dragging that carcass.
Released from the mechanism of a bow, he pierced him in an instant;
that boy was carried off by the Bhilla children,
while I, having fallen into a swoon, was taken away by someone.
Having been brought by Vṛṣṇipāla and led into his own hut,
her wounds were treated with compassion; once she had recovered and wished to attend upon her husband, she remained there for a while due to her lack of assistance.
I was still in a state of agitation when my own daughter arrived at that very spot with some young man;
she wept bitterly.

At the end of her weeping, she related how, during the destruction of the caravan, the prince who had been in her own hands had come into the hands of the Kirāta leader, and how she herself had had her wounds healed by a certain forest-dweller; and once she was restored to health—
Furthermore, he thought of approaching her again; however,
because of his agitation caused by contact with a low-born caste, she had spoken harsh words of rejection, which he could not endure.
She related that, having seen this youth by chance in a secluded forest as he was making an effort to cut off his own head, there would follow the slaying of that wicked man and her own marriage.
But he, being questioned, turned out to be a certain servant of the Lord of Mithilā who had been delayed for some reason and was following his path;
together with him, he approached his master and [reported] the news regarding his son.
We two heard of this from the mouth of the goddess and from Priyamvadā;
and that king, due to the fault of fate, for a long time [was separated] from his eldest sons.
Furthermore, having engaged in hostilities and fought excessively for a long time out of intolerance, he was captured,
and the queen was also led into captivity.
"Though I am consumed by grief even in this old age, being unable to cast off my wretched life, I have indeed taken up the life of renunciation;
yet my daughter has been drawn away by her own miserable existence."
It is said that he took as his consort Kalpasundarī, the chief queen of Vikaṭavarman;
had those two princes grown up without any misfortune, [the outcome would have been different].

"In this much time, these two would have reached this stage of life for you; and while they were present, the heirs of the king would not have been able to act with such violence. Thus, overcome with grief, he wept aloud.
Having heard the words of the female ascetic, my tears also welled up, and I spoke secretly: "If it is so, mother, take heart;
surely there is some sage who, while you were in that state..."
Requested by him for the sake of obtaining sons, he was obtained and raised;
this is a very great matter.
What is the use of this?
I am he; and it is possible for me.
This Vikatavarman has somehow managed to approach me in order to kill me;
furthermore, his younger brothers are very numerous, and they too are plotting against me.
The people of the city and the countryside—
no one here knows me for who I am;
even my parents do not recognize me, let alone others.
"I shall accomplish this matter by some means," I said.
But that old woman, embracing me with tears and repeatedly smelling my head, her breasts flowing with milk, spoke in a faltering voice: "My child!"
Live long! May it be well with you!
Today the Blessed Lord Vidhi is pleased.
This very day, the kingdom of Videha has truly come under Prahāravarmā’s dominion,
since you, with your long and stout arms, now stand ready to carry us across this shoreless ocean of grief.
"Oh, how great is the good fortune of the lady Priyamvadā! exclaiming thus, she attended to me with baths, food, and other comforts, being overflowing with joy;
and I took up residence for the night in a corner of this monastery.
On my bed of straw, I thought: "This objective cannot be accomplished without a stratagem;
and women are the breeding ground for stratagems."
"Therefore, having learned the news from the inner apartments, I shall employ some stratagem through her means"— while I was still thinking thus,
she was shaken, as it were, by the speed of the breath of the horses of the sun emerging from the great ocean.
The night withdrew;
the maker of day appeared with diminished splendor, as if numbed by dwelling within the womb of the intense darkness.
Having risen and completed the daily rites and observances of the morning,
I said to my mother: "Mother, do you know anything of the affairs of the harem of that wretch Vikatavarman?"
Even as my speech remained unfinished, a certain woman appeared before me; and upon seeing her, my nurse [spoke].
With her throat choked by tears of joy, she said: "Daughter Puṣkarikā, look at the prince!
This very man, whom I mercilessly abandoned in the forest, has been found again."
"He has arrived thus.
But she, overwhelmed by a flood of joy, wept for a long time and lamented much; then, having been comforted, she was again addressed by her mother.
She was appointed to recount the affairs of the royal harem,
and she said: "O Prince, there is the daughter of Kalindavarman, the lord of Kāmarūpa, named Kalpasundarī, who is peerless in the arts and in beauty."
"And she surpasses even the Apsarases, for she dwells having overcome her husband; thus,
although Vikaṭavarman has many wives in his harem, she alone is his beloved."
I said to her: "Approach her with perfumes and garlands sent by me,
and incite her to find fault with her own husband by pointing out his unequalled defects."
And instill resentment by describing Vāsavadattā and others who have gone to suitably matched husbands.
"Furthermore, by diligently searching for and publicizing even the most secret amorous sports of the king within his inner apartments, increase her pride."
Again, I said this to my mother: "In this very manner, you too must attend upon this queen, with no other occupation;
and whatever occurs there day by day, I shall [inform you]."

She must be enlightened by you alone; moreover, this [instruction] spoken by me is like an inseparable shadow for the accomplishment of our karma, which is sweet in its ultimate result, as it pertains to Kalpasundarī.
"Let it be observed," she said; and they both carried out that matter exactly as instructed.
After some days had passed, my mother said to me:
"My child, she has been so managed and established that she will consider herself pitiable, like a mādhavī creeper clinging to a neem tree;
what more remains to be done?"
Furthermore, having painted my own likeness, I shall say: "This is to be taken to such-and-such a person"; and when she has seen it once it has been delivered, she will certainly speak thus.
"If there indeed exists some man of such a form," she says—answer her thus: "If he should exist, what of it?
Whatever answer she gives to that, I am that.
"He is to be awakened.
She replied, "So be it," and having approached the royal palace and returned, she informed me in private: "My child, he has been shown to him."
He gave that painted cloth to that intoxicated woman;
and she, being filled with wonder, thought: "This world has been truly blessed, since even the god whose bow is made of flowers [Kāma] is present here."
Such beauty of form is not present [elsewhere];
this is wonderful, even more wonderful!
And I do not know anyone belonging to this world who could create such a thing.
"By whom was this painted? she asked with respect and spoke thus. And I, with a smile, replied: "O Queen, you speak what is fitting."
It is impossible even to conceive that the Blessed One Makaraketu could be so beautiful; nevertheless,
this ocean-bound earth is vast.
In some cases, even such a form as this might come into being through the power of fate;
yet, if there were a youth of such a form, possessing skill in arts, character, learning, and knowledge corresponding to his appearance—
"If some man of noble birth were present here, what would he receive?
She replied, "Mother, what can I say?"
The body, the heart, and life— all of this is trifling and unworthy;
therefore, nothing at all will be gained from it.
"If this is not a deception, then a favor should be rendered such that, through the experience of seeing him, this eye may become fulfilled."
Furthermore, I proposed this in order to strengthen my position: "There is a certain prince wandering in disguise;
at this spring festival, he was with his female companions..."
Like Rati incarnate, sporting in the city grove, you have by chance come within the range of my vision;
and he, that sole target for the arrows of Kama, has likewise come to me.
And I, being impelled by you two— who were mutually suited to one another in terms of rare physical forms and other such preeminent qualities— consented.
For a long time you have been worshipped with flower-garlands, ointments, and other offerings fashioned by him alone;
and he himself has depicted his own likeness here.
He was sent to demonstrate the depth of your meditative absorption;
if this matter is certain, then for that person of superhuman vitality, courage, and excellence of wisdom, it is not so.
"There is indeed a certain difficult task;
I shall demonstrate it this very day.
An appointment must be made."
Having reflected for a moment, she spoke again: "Mother, this is not something to be kept most secret from you now;
therefore, I shall tell you."
My father had great affection for King Praharavarman,
and Queen Mānavatī was a dear friend of my mother.
Priyamvadā was there.
Furthermore, while they were still childless, they made an agreement: "Whichever of us two has a son shall give him to the daughter of the other."
"The daughter must be given," [he said]. But my father, by a stroke of fate, gave me— who had been born as Priyamvadā— to Vikaṭavarman, who was seeking a child since his own offspring had perished.
He gave [it];
and this man is cruel, a traitor to his father, and not one whose disposition is very well-disposed toward the refinements of sensual pleasure.
Lacking proficiency in the arts such as poetry and drama,
he is sluggish in his application; intoxicated by his own valor, he is boastful,
a speaker of falsehoods, and one who rains down [rewards] at the wrong time.
This husband of mine does not please me, especially during these days,
since he has Puṣkarikā— who is as intimate to me as my own self— [in the garden].

Furthermore, there is one named Ramayantika, who stands near me, yet disregards me; she is ignorant of her own nature, harbors the resentment of a co-wife toward me, and is merely an actress in her own drama.

He honored Campakalatā, whom he had raised as if she were his own child, by personally decorating her with *sumanaḥ* flowers that he himself had gathered, treating her no differently than his own offspring.
He sported with her upon a jeweled couch situated within the inner altar of Citrakūṭa, which had been enjoyed and vacated by me;
and that unworthy man proceeded even to treat her with contempt.
What need is there to ask why? For the fear of the next world is obscured by the suffering of this life;
indeed, the touch of women, like the quiver of arrows upon the body, is unbearable.
For those whose hearts are true, there is the suffering of being constrained by dwelling with an undesirable person;
therefore, let this man join me today in the Mādhavī bower of the garden.
For my mind has become exceedingly attached merely by hearing news of him;
and here is this heap of wealth.
"Having established him in such-and-such a position, I shall live by serving him exclusively.
Having agreed to that, I returned.
"Beyond this, the prince is the authority," she said.
Then, from her very presence, [he learned] of the layout of the inner apartments, the positions of the eunuchs, and the various regions of the pleasure groves.
Furthermore, as the orb of the sun turns crimson, as if its blood were stirred by its fall upon the peak of the western mountain, it is perceived through its distinct divisions.

When the darkness had spread, filling the sky like a mass of smoke from the embers of the sun extinguished by the pouring of the waters of the western ocean, [the moon] rose as if to act as my preceptor in my intent to violate another's wife.
The moon, the foremost of planets, who delights in embracing his preceptor,
was smiling as if with the lotus-face of Kalpasundarī, which had first approached him out of an excess of passion upon seeing me.
While the god whose bow is flowers— his splendor kindled by the lunar orb and intent on conquering the world— was engaged in his task, I took to my bed as was appropriate.
And he reflected further: "This matter is already as good as accomplished;
however, by violating another's wife, there would be an injury to dharma.
Yet even that [injury] occurs when both artha and kāma are attained."
"It is indeed approved by the authors of the treatises;
and as for this transgression committed by me through the intention of finding a means to release my elders from their bonds— even that sin, having been expiated by [this much]..."
"May he unite me with a portion of his merit.
However, having heard this, Rājavāhana, the king, was overcome by sleep while lost in the thought, "What indeed will my friends say upon hearing this?"
I touched it, and in a dream the Blessed One with the face of an elephant appeared;
he said: "O gentle Upahāravarman, let it not be so for you."
A false conception has arisen,
since you are but a portion of me;
for that celestial river is accustomed only to being cherished by the mass of Śaṅkara’s matted locks.
She was a woman of excellent complexion. Once, unable to endure my agitation, she cursed me, saying:
"Come, enter the state of a mortal!"

And I cursed her, saying: "Just as you are to be enjoyed by many here, so even after attaining human birth, may you become common to many. And she entreated me, saying: "May I have you alone as my husband once more."
"Having served him in this way, may I rejoice for as long as I live"—
this purpose is indeed worthy of being undertaken by you without hesitation.
And having awakened, filled with joy, he spent that day as well.
I spent the time remembering the tryst with my beloved and other such matters;
on another day, the god of love, acting without deviation, rained down his arrows upon me alone.
The lake consisting of light belonging to the radiant one dried up, while the mire consisting of darkness spread forth; and he,
clad in garments of mud, tightened his firm girdle.
With sword in hand and equipped with the necessary implements, remembering the tokens given by my mother, I approached the moat of the royal palace which was filled to the brim with water.
Then, at the gate of Mātṛgṛha, Upakhāta took the bamboo pole that Puṣkarikā had previously prepared; with it he filled the moat and established a wall against the rampart.
Having ascended the impassable ground by means of a flight of stairs built of baked bricks that led up to the upper surface of the city gate, he reached the earth.
I descended; having descended and passed through the street of *vakula* trees,
I approached slightly by way of the path of the *campaka* rows toward the north.
I heard the plaintive cry of a pair of ruddy geese;
then, turning northward along a path lined with trumpet-flowers,
I proceeded for the distance of an arrow-shot through the interior of a spacious palace wall that could be reached by touch.
Having gone as it were, and having again traversed a short distance further north by a sandy path whose two sides were adorned with clusters of *piṇḍī-bhāṇḍīra* trees, once more—
I entered the southern row of mango trees,
and from there, a more dense bower of mādhavī creepers, in whose interior a jeweled altar had been constructed.
I discerned it by the light of a lamp-wick emerging from a slightly opened casket;
and having entered, I stood at one side.
The inner sanctum was enclosed by walls consisting of rows of kuraṇṭaka shrubs densely covered with blossoming flowers,
while it was adorned with young shoots of tender buds resembling fresh coral-tree creepers fallen upon the ground.
Having opened the door, which was rosy with a mass of fresh young shoots,
I entered; and there lay a well-spread bed of flowers.
There were lotus-leaf cups containing materials for writing, an ivory fan,
and a golden pitcher filled with fragrant water.
Having sat down for a moment, I rested and inhaled an exceeding fragrance;
then I heard the very soft sound of footsteps.
As soon as I heard this, I emerged from the trysting-house and stood with my body concealed by the side of the trunk of a red aśoka tree.
And that woman of beautiful brows, longing for Asuṣīma, approached there slowly; not seeing me there,
she was deeply distressed and let out a cry like a rutting royal female swan.
With a voice faltering and choked with emotion in her throat, she said: "Clearly I have been deceived;
there is no way for me to live."
O heart, why do you thus distress yourself by superimposing this improper act upon what is proper, when such a thing is impossible?
O Blessed One, the five-arrowed god has committed an offense against you through me.

"That you burn him thus, yet do not reduce him to ashes. Then, manifesting myself with the vessel of a lamp held open, I said: "O beautiful lady, have you not indeed committed a great offense against the Mind-born [Cupid], since—"

For him, Rati has become his very life; his bow-staff is rendered redundant by the beauty of his form; the bowstring made of a swarm of bees is surpassed by the luster of his dark tresses; and his weapons are [the marks] of his eyebrows.
With showers of sidelong glances,
he [the elephant] was like a first friend to the silk banner-cloth of the safflower-dyed flag, with the masses of rays from his tusks.
The Malaya breeze with her breath more fragrant than its own scent;
the song of the cuckoo with her exceedingly sweet chatter; and the banner made of flowers with her two lotus-stalk-like arms.
Her pair of breasts was a pair of full jars for the commencement of her world conquest; her navel-region was a pleasure-pool;
and her hip-region was an armored chariot.
With your pair of thighs, you are the two pillars for the archway of the jewels of existence;
with the radiance of your soles, you are the playful sprouts upon the ears [of that arch].
Therefore, it is only in this very place that the fish-bannered god (Kāma) torments you.
But that he should trouble me excessively, though I am without fault, is his own fault alone.
Therefore, be gracious, O beautiful one, and restore me to life with the medicines of life.
As if bitten by the serpent of the bodiless one (Kāma) with his sidelong glances,
he embraced her; and he took his pleasure with her, whose large eyes were as lovely as the unguents of the bodiless one.
Her purpose accomplished, her eyes reddened and rolling,
the roots of her cheeks marred by the emergence of slight lines of perspiration, she uttered indistinct and broken lamentations.
Perceiving her— whose body was exceedingly relaxed due to the contact of the application of his reddish teeth and nails— to be as if afflicted,
he slackened both his mental and physical concentration.
Making even himself share in that same purpose,
they experienced the ritual at the conclusion of their pleasure as if it were long-familiar, with a deeply hidden intimacy born from a bond released at that very moment.
"Let us stay for a moment. Again, sighing hot and long breaths with a somewhat dejected look, [he spoke] with hands stretched out tremulously.
Embracing her with my arms without pressing too hard, I kissed her without being too clear;
but she, with tears on her face, said: "O Lord, if you depart, then let this [tear] depart."
Count my life as well; take me too,
for this servant is not without purpose.
Thus he brought her hands together in the gesture of salutation;
and I said to her, "O innocent girl, what conscious being [would not do so]?"
He does not welcome a woman who desires him. If your intention is fixed upon favoring me, then act without hesitation according to my instruction.
Show the king in private a painted canvas containing my likeness,
and say to him: "Is this form the very essence of male beauty?"
"Has she reached the further shore or not?
"Certainly she has reached it," he will surely say.
Speak further: "If this is so, is there some female ascetic [who knows]?"
"She, who has become like a mother to me and has gained confidence through traveling in foreign lands,
placed this painted image before me and said:"
"There exists such a mantra by which you, having fasted on the sacred day,
alone at night upon a secluded spot of ground where the seven-flamed fire has been fed and consecrated by the priests, [should offer] a hundred sticks of sandalwood."
Having offered handfuls of camphor and abundant silk garments, you will come to have such a form;
then you shall ring the bell.
And when your husband, summoned by the ringing of the bell,
has revealed all secrets to you and embraces you with eyes closed, this form shall pass over to him.
"But you shall become exactly as you were before,
provided this pleases you and your beloved, and no contradiction should be made regarding this arrangement."
If this body is indeed dear to you,
then having deliberated with your friends, ministers, younger brothers, and the people of the city and the countryside, proceed toward this task with their approval as well.

furthermore, in this very courtyard of the pleasure-grove bower—

Having offered oblations with a sacrificial animal consecrated according to the Atharvanic rite, once the fire has been extinguished, I shall remain in this very bower of creepers, having entered it through the impurity of its smoke.
Furthermore, at the hour of deep nightfall,
you shall whisper into the ear of Vikaṭavarman with a playful smile:
"You are a rogue and ungrateful."
"Even with this form obtained through my grace, which serves as a festival for the eyes of the world, you shall delight my rivals;

Thus,
having heard these words of yours, you shall come to me alone and report whatever he says.
"Beyond this, I myself shall know;
meanwhile, have my footprints wiped away from the grove by Puṣkarikā.
She, saying "So be it," treated my words with the same respect as the instruction of a teacher.
Like one whose passion for love-play was not yet satiated, she entered the inner apartments with great difficulty;
I too, having exited by the same way I had entered, went to my own dwelling.
"I have gone.
Then that beautiful woman acted accordingly toward him,
and that evil-minded man remained compliant with her will.
And this wonderful report spread among the citizens and the people of the countryside: "It is said that King Vikaṭavarman will, by the power of the queen's mantras,
attain a body worthy of a god."
Surely this is a deception; it is not at all auspicious.
What talk can there be of negligence?
[This has happened] right here in the inner garden of his own harem, by none other than his own chief queen.
Indeed, this matter is to be accomplished;
for it has been deliberated upon and approved even by ministers whose intellects are equal to Bṛhaspati.
If it is thus, there is nothing more wonderful than this;
for the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is indeed inconceivable.
While such rumors were spreading among the people, on the arrival of the festival day,
at the hour of nightfall when the thick darkness had set in,
he emerged from the garden of the inner apartments.
The smoke rising from the throat of Dhūrjaṭi, as grey as smoke itself, and the fragrance of oblations consisting of milk, clarified butter, curds, sesame, white mustard, fat, meat, and blood,
followed by the wind, spread in every direction.
It rained; and when that rising of smoke had suddenly subsided, I entered,
and the woman who moves with the gait of an elephant arrived at the palace garden.
And embracing me with a smile, he said: "O rogue, your desire is accomplished;
that sacrificial animal has been finished."
To entice him, I spoke according to your instructions: "O gambler, I do not fail to acknowledge your beauty;
for you are so handsome that even the Apsarases would envy you."
"How much less so for human women?
A cruel man like you, as naturally fickle as a bee, clings to anyone and everyone."
But he, having fallen at my feet, said: "O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, endure the misdeeds committed by me;
from this moment forth, I shall not even think of another woman in my mind."
"Hurry with the task at hand! Thus,
I have come to you in such a bridal attire.
Even before this, she was given to you by the great God of Love, with the fire of passion as witness; now once again, making this very fire of birth (Jātavedas) your witness—
Saying, "It has been given by my own heart," she pressed her forefoot against the instep of his foot and, lifting her heel,
pressed him with the tender leaf-like fingers of her other foot, which were interlaced with one another.
Gently encircling my neck with her two creeper-like arms and bending my face toward her own, she gazed with wide, wandering eyes at the lotus of her face which she had herself raised.
He kissed her repeatedly.
Then he said to her, "Stay right here within the thicket of *kuraṇṭaka* shrubs until I have gone out and properly accomplished what is to be done."
Having dismissed her and approached the place of the sacrificial fire,
I rang the bell hanging from the branch of an *aśoka* tree;
and it made that person cry out.
Like a messenger of Death summoning me,
I began to offer incense led by aloe and sandalwood;
and the king arrived at the place as described.
Seeing him standing there as if seized by doubt, reflecting with some astonishment, I said: "Speak the truth once more to me,
even while making the venerable Citrabhānu himself your witness."
"If you do not delight my co-wives with this form, then I shall transfer this form onto you.
At that very moment, he thought, "This is surely the Goddess herself; it is no deception."
With a clear conviction having arisen within me, I proceeded to take an oath.
Smiling, I spoke again: "What is the use of an oath?
For what mere mortal woman could possibly despise me?"
"If you associate with the Apsarases, associate as you please; however, tell me what your secrets are, for at the conclusion of that disclosure, your true form will surely vanish."
He said: "My father's younger brother, Prahāravarmā, is imprisoned.
Having caused him to die by means of poisoned food, [one must falsely report] the fault of indigestion."
"I shall proclaim [this]"— thus it was resolved by the ministers together.
The army circle (daṇḍacakra) was intended to be given to his younger brother Viśālavarman for the purpose of marching against the Puṇḍra country.
The city elder Pāñcālika and the caravan leader Paritrāta obtained from a Yavana named Khanati a single diamond, worth the entire earth, for a very small price.
They both addressed me in private;
and the householder Śatahali, who was my intimate associate and a great man of the land, was of a character prone to false speech.

"I shall have the arrogant and wicked village headman Anantasīra killed by the wrath of the people," he said, and thus consented to employ the wielders of the rod [the executioners] in the act of his removal.
Having heard these words— "Such is this secret that has just been revealed"— he [the king] said to him,
"This much is your lifespan;
depart for the state appropriate to your own karma," and with a small knife...
Having cut it into two pieces, I offered them as oblations right there into that fire of golden flames, in which clarified butter was flowing in abundance;
and it was reduced to ashes.
Then, having comforted his beloved who was slightly distressed by her feminine nature, and taking hold of her sprout-like hand,
he went to her house; and with her permission, [he entered] all...
Having summoned the women of the inner apartments, he immediately offered them his service;
after spending some time in the midst of the circle of astonished courtesans, he dismissed the assembly of the harem and returned to her alone.
Embracing her with my thighs pressed against her thighs and my arms pressed against her arms, I delighted her upon the couch and passed that night as if it were but a short moment.
And from his mouth I learned the character of that royal family.
Having bathed at dawn and performed the auspicious rites, I met with the ministers and said to them: "Noble sirs, along with their very appearance..."
My own disposition has been transformed. This father of mine, who was intended to be killed by poisoned food,
must be released and made to accept this kingdom of his once again.
"In that matter, we shall conduct ourselves solely through service toward him as toward a father;
for there is no sin greater than the murder of a father.
And having summoned his brother Viśālavarman, he said:
"My child, the Puṇḍras are not currently well-supplied with food.
Stricken by suffering and delusion, they will abandon their own lives and attack our prosperous kingdom."
"Therefore, when the destruction of the granaries or the destruction of the crops occurs,
then you shall march; an expedition today is not appropriate."
I also spoke to the two elders of the city: "Let not this highly precious diamond be obtained by me for a very small price;
rather, let it be mine for a price commensurate with its value, for the sake of protecting the Dharma."
"Let it be done," he said;
